key_results: Full pinning at degree ten: in the uniform-Frobenius model for Q(ζ₁₁), the Frobenius type T(p) = ord₁₁(p) takes the values 1, 2, 5, 10 with densities 1/10, 1/10, 4/10, 4/10, and I(p mod 11; T) = H(T) = log₂5 − 3/5 ≈ 1.72193 bits, with H(T | p mod 11) = 0 and H(p mod 11 | T) = 8/5 exactly.

# Eleven Clocks and a Single Remainder: How One Number Tells You Everything About a Prime's Fate

*The tenth rung of the abelian ladder — the full cyclotomic field built from the eleventh roots of unity — confirms a striking law: in an abelian world, a prime's remainder knows its entire destiny.*

---

## A prime walks into a bigger number system

Pick a prime number, say $p = 3$. In the ordinary integers it is indivisible — that is what "prime" means. But mathematicians have long known that primes behave differently when you enlarge the number system. Throw in $i = \sqrt{-1}$, and $5$ suddenly factors as $(2+i)(2-i)$, while $3$ stays stubbornly whole. Primes that were atoms in one world can shatter into fragments in another.

The question of *how* a prime breaks apart — into how many pieces, and of what size — is called its **splitting type**. For about two centuries, number theorists have treated splitting types as the fingerprints of number fields. In modern cryptography the same structures quietly underpin lattice-based schemes built over cyclotomic rings, where the way the polynomial $x^n + 1$ or $\Phi_m(x)$ falls apart modulo a prime decides how fast multiplication can be done and how the algebra decomposes.

This article is about one specific enlarged world — the field generated by an eleventh root of unity, written $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ — and about a crisp information-theoretic fact: **the remainder $p \bmod 11$ carries every last bit of information about how $p$ splits.** Not most of it. All of it, exactly $\log_2 5 - 3/5 \approx 1.7219$ bits.

## The eleventh roots of unity

Picture a clock with eleven equally spaced marks on the unit circle in the complex plane. The mark at angle $2\pi/11$ is the number $\zeta_{11} = e^{2\pi i/11}$, and the other marks are its powers $\zeta_{11}^2, \zeta_{11}^3, \dots$. All ten non-trivial marks are roots of a single polynomial,

$$\Phi_{11}(x) = x^{10} + x^9 + \cdots + x + 1,$$

the eleventh **cyclotomic polynomial** ("circle-dividing"). Adjoining $\zeta_{11}$ to the rational numbers produces a number system of dimension $10$ — degree ten.

The symmetries of this system are wonderfully simple. Any symmetry must send $\zeta_{11}$ to another primitive eleventh root $\zeta_{11}^a$, with $a \in \{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$, and composing symmetries multiplies the exponents modulo $11$. So the symmetry group — the Galois group — is just the group of nonzero remainders modulo $11$ under multiplication, written $(\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$. It is a cyclic group of order ten: every element is a power of $2$, since the powers $2, 4, 8, 5, 10, 9, 7, 3, 6, 1$ run through all ten remainders.

## Frobenius: the prime's own symmetry

Here is the miracle that makes everything work. For each prime $p \neq 11$, there is a distinguished symmetry, the **Frobenius element** of $p$, and in cyclotomic fields it is as concrete as can be: it is the symmetry $\zeta_{11} \mapsto \zeta_{11}^{p}$. In other words, the Frobenius of $p$ *is* the remainder $p \bmod 11$.

And the Frobenius controls the splitting. If $t$ is the **order** of $p$ modulo $11$ — the smallest $t \ge 1$ with $p^t \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$ — then $p$ breaks into $10/t$ prime fragments, each of "size" (residue degree) $t$. Since $t$ must divide $10$, there are exactly four possible fates:

| order $t$ | remainders $p \bmod 11$ | fate of $p$ | how $\Phi_{11}$ factors mod $p$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $1$ | splits completely into 10 pieces | ten linear factors $[1^{10}]$ |
| $2$ | $10$ | 5 pieces of size 2 | five quadratics $[2^5]$ |
| $5$ | $3, 4, 5, 9$ | 2 pieces of size 5 | two quintics $[5,5]$ |
| $10$ | $2, 6, 7, 8$ | stays prime (inert) | irreducible $[10]$ |

Call this order the **Frobenius type** $T(p)$. The last column is the down-to-earth version: you can see a prime's type simply by factoring the polynomial $\Phi_{11}(x)$ with coefficients reduced modulo $p$. Over $\mathbb{F}_{23}$ (and $23 \equiv 1$) it splits into ten linear pieces; over $\mathbb{F}_{43}$ ($43 \equiv -1$) into five quadratics; over $\mathbb{F}_3$ into two quintics; over $\mathbb{F}_2$ it does not factor at all.

## How often does each fate occur?

A classical theorem — Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions, a special case of the Chebotarev density theorem — says primes are equidistributed among the ten remainders mod $11$. So each remainder occurs with probability $1/10$, and the four types occur with probabilities

$$\Pr[T=1] = \tfrac{1}{10},\quad \Pr[T=2] = \tfrac{1}{10},\quad \Pr[T=5] = \tfrac{4}{10},\quad \Pr[T=10] = \tfrac{4}{10}.$$

There is a beautiful reason behind the numbers $1, 1, 4, 4$: in a cyclic group of order $n$, the number of elements of order $d$ is Euler's totient $\varphi(d)$ — and indeed $\varphi(1)=1$, $\varphi(2)=1$, $\varphi(5)=4$, $\varphi(10)=4$. This holds for every cyclic Galois group, so every cyclic field has type densities $\varphi(d)/n$.

The prediction was tested against **295,946 unramified primes**, and the observed frequencies sat right on top of $1/10, 1/10, 4/10, 4/10$.

## Measuring "how much the remainder knows"

Now for the information theory. Claude Shannon taught us to measure uncertainty in **bits**. If a random quantity $X$ takes values with probabilities $q_1, q_2, \dots$, its entropy is

$$H(X) = -\sum_i q_i \log_2 q_i.$$

The Frobenius type has entropy

$$H(T) = -2\cdot\tfrac{1}{10}\log_2\tfrac{1}{10} - 2\cdot\tfrac{4}{10}\log_2\tfrac{4}{10} = \log_2 5 - \tfrac{3}{5} \approx 1.7219 \text{ bits}.$$

That is how uncertain you are about a random prime's fate before learning anything.

The **mutual information** $I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y)$ measures how many of those bits a second observation $Y$ reveals. Think of a "channel": the remainder $p \bmod 11$ goes in, and we ask how much of the type $T(p)$ comes out.

**The degree-ten full-pinning theorem.** *For primes with uniformly distributed Frobenius in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$,*
$$I(p \bmod 11;\ T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac{3}{5} \approx 1.7219 \text{ bits, exactly}.$$
*Moreover, the type is completely determined once the remainder is known — $H(T \mid p \bmod 11) = 0$ — while the type leaves exactly $H(p \bmod 11 \mid T) = 8/5$ bits of the remainder undetermined.*

The intuition is short: the type is a *function* of the remainder (the order of $p \bmod 11$), so knowing the remainder leaves no doubt about the type. The remainder has $\log_2 10 \approx 3.32$ bits, and exactly $1.72$ of them are "about the type"; the remaining $1.6$ bits distinguish, say, $3$ from $4$ from $5$ from $9$ — remainders that share the same fate.

The precise decimals are not left to floating-point luck: from exact integer comparisons such as $2^{23219} < 5^{10000}$ and $5^{100000} < 2^{232193}$ one gets $2.3219 < \log_2 5 < 2.32193$, and hence the certified enclosure
$$1.7219 < I(p \bmod 11;\ T) < 1.72193.$$

## Why abelian is the magic word

Why should this be true, and how far does it extend? The real engine is a general law.

**The abelian full-pinning law.** *Let the Galois group $A$ be any finite abelian group, let $c$ be any readout that tells all elements of $A$ apart (like the remainder), and let $T$ be any splitting-type readout. Then the residue pins the type: $I(c;T) = H(T)$; the type is certain given the residue: $H(T \mid c) = 0$; and the information lost is exactly the residual uncertainty: $\log_2|A| - I(c;T) = H(c \mid T)$.*

In a non-abelian world things are different. There, the most an "abelian" residue can see is the image of Frobenius in the *abelianization* — the group with all commutators crushed to the identity. Different Frobenius classes can look identical through that lens, and the residue then fails to pin the type. Abelian fields are exactly those where nothing is crushed: the residue is a perfect label.

This single law covers every rung of the "abelian ladder" checked so far — fields of degree $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9$ and now $10$, built both as real subfields of cyclotomic fields and as full cyclotomic fields — with no exceptions, because it is a theorem about *all* abelian groups at once.

## A ladder inside the ladder: the real subfield and one extra bit

$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ contains a degree-five subfield made of real numbers, generated by $\zeta_{11} + \zeta_{11}^{-1} = 2\cos(2\pi/11)$. Its Galois group is $(\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times / \{\pm 1\}$, cyclic of order five, and the type $T^+(p)$ there is the order of $p$ up to sign. Two remainders ($\pm1$) give type $1$; the other eight give type $5$. So

$$H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac{8}{5} \approx 0.7219 \text{ bits},$$

and the same remainder pins this type too. Going up from the real subfield to the full field adds **exactly one bit** of type information: $H(T \mid T^+) = 1$, matching $\log_2$ of the degree $[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11}) : \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+] = 2$.

There is an elegant explanation via the Chinese Remainder Theorem: the cyclic group of order $10$ is a product $C_2 \times C_5$, the order of an element is the product of the orders of its two components, and the two components are independent. Entropy adds over independent pieces, so

$$H(T) = H_{C_2} + H_{C_5} = 1 + \left(\log_2 5 - \tfrac{8}{5}\right).$$

## From four hundred checks to every prime

The polynomial side was tested on 400 primes: in every case, the degrees of the irreducible factors of $\Phi_{11}$ mod $p$ matched the predicted pattern. (A small cautionary tale from the computation: the first comparison reported 400 mismatches out of 400 — not because the mathematics failed, but because one side wrapped the pattern in an extra layer of brackets. The pattern itself was perfect.)

The experiment can now be retired in favor of a theorem valid for **every prime and every conductor**:

**Factor-pattern theorem.** *For any $n$ and any prime $p$ not dividing $n$, the polynomial $\Phi_n(x)$ factors over $\mathbb{F}_p$ into exactly $\varphi(n)/t$ irreducible factors, each of degree $t$, where $t$ is the order of $p$ modulo $n$.* 

There is a lovely mirror image inside the group: multiplying the elements of $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$ by $p$ shuffles them into cycles, and every cycle has length exactly $t$, with $\varphi(n)/t$ cycles in all. The factorization of the polynomial is the cycle structure of the permutation. A consequence: if $p \equiv q \pmod n$, then $\Phi_n$ factors with the same pattern modulo $p$ and modulo $q$ — the remainder alone determines the shape.

## Semiprimes: when two fates multiply

Cryptographers care about numbers like $N = pq$, products of two primes. Suppose we observe only $N \bmod 11$. How much do we learn about the *pair* of fates $\{T(p), T(q)\}$?

Model $p$ and $q$ as having independent, uniformly distributed remainders. The remainder of $N$ is the product of the two remainders, and multiplication mixes things up: $N \equiv 1$ could come from $1\cdot 1$, from $10 \cdot 10$, from $3 \cdot 4$, and so on. The exact answer is

$$I\big(N \bmod 11;\ \{T(p),T(q)\}\big) = \log_2 5 + \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \tfrac{47}{25} \approx 1.20271 \text{ bits}.$$

This value has a story. An empirical measurement returned $1.2002$; an enumeration produced $1.1999$; and an earlier closed-form calculation predicted $1.2027$. The exact law settles the matter: it lies within $3 \times 10^{-5}$ of $1.2027$ and strictly above both $1.2002$ and $1.1999$. The earlier closed form was right; the other two figures were finite-sample estimates, and the apparent "wall" of $0.0005$ between them is just the gap between two estimates, not a feature of the mathematics.

Comparing with the single-prime channel gives a clean **attenuation law**:

$$H(T) - I\big(N \bmod 11;\ \{T(p),T(q)\}\big) = \tfrac{32}{25} - \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 \approx 0.519 \text{ bits}.$$

Multiplying two primes together blurs about half a bit of fate information.

## The wall that isn't there

One more question: does it help to know *which* prime has which type — the ordered pair $(T(p), T(q))$ rather than the unordered set? Remarkably, no. At degree ten the ordered and unordered channels carry *exactly* the same information about $N \bmod 11$. This "which-factor wall" is zero.

And it is zero for a structural reason that reaches far beyond degree ten. Swapping $p$ and $q$ leaves $N$ unchanged but swaps the ordered pair. A neat entropy lemma shows that forgetting the order of a swap-symmetric pair costs exactly the probability that the two entries differ — and it costs that *same* amount whether or not you also know $N$. The two costs cancel in the mutual information. The only requirement is that the residue cannot tell $gh$ from $hg$. In an abelian group that is automatic. In a non-abelian group it still holds whenever the residue is read through the abelianization, because $gh$ and $hg$ differ by a commutator. This explains in one stroke why previously computed which-factor walls for the non-abelian groups $A_4$ (the rotations of a tetrahedron) and $D_4$ (the symmetries of a square) were also exactly zero.

## What the tenth rung teaches

Step back and the picture is satisfying. Every prediction made in advance for degree ten came true: the densities $1,1,4,4$ out of ten; the full-pinning value $\log_2 5 - 3/5$; the per-class certainty; the factor patterns. Two predictions were upgraded from "checked on data" to "true always": the polynomial patterns now hold for every prime and every conductor, and the zero which-factor wall holds for every group read through its abelianization. And one number was corrected: the semiprime law is $1.20271$, not the enumerated $1.1999$.

The broader lesson is about what "knowing the remainder" means. In an abelian number field, a prime's remainder is not a hint about its fate — it *is* its fate, written in a different alphabet. The remainder holds a few extra bits beyond that (exactly $8/5$ of them at degree ten), but nothing about the splitting is left unknown. The frontier now moves to non-abelian fields — where the residue sees only a shadow of the Frobenius — and to open conjectures: that the gap between a cyclotomic field and its real subfield is always a power of two, namely $2^{1 - v_2(p-1)}$ bits, and that multiplying primes always blurs fate information for every prime conductor $\ell \ge 5$.

Eleven marks on a circle, ten symmetries, four fates — and one remainder that knows them all.

# Full Pinning at Degree Ten: Exact Type Channels of the Cyclotomic Field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

For a Galois number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ and an unramified prime $p$, the *Frobenius type* records how $p$ splits in $K$. We study the information-theoretic channel from a residue observation (such as $p \bmod n$) to the Frobenius type, in the model where Frobenius classes are uniformly distributed (Chebotarev). For the full cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$, of degree ten with cyclic Galois group $C_{10} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$, we prove that the residue $p \bmod 11$ *fully pins* the type: the mutual information equals the type entropy,
$$I(p \bmod 11;\ T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35 \approx 1.72193,$$
the type is certain given the residue, and the residue retains exactly $8/5$ bits given the type. These follow from a general *abelian full-pinning law* valid for every finite abelian Galois group, together with a closed form $H(T) = -\sum_{d\mid n} \frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\log_2\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}$ for every cyclic field. We prove that for every $n$ and every prime $p \nmid n$ the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$ factors over $\mathbb{F}_p$ into $\varphi(n)/t$ irreducible factors of degree $t = \operatorname{ord}_n(p)$, and that this is the cycle pattern of multiplication by $p$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$. We analyse the tower $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+ \subset \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$, showing that the real quintic subfield is also fully pinned with $H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - 8/5$ and that the tower contributes exactly one bit. For semiprimes $N = pq$ we obtain the exact channel $I(N \bmod 11;\ \{T(p),T(q)\}) = \log_2 5 + \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \frac{47}{25} \approx 1.20271$, an exact attenuation of $\frac{32}{25} - \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3 \approx 0.519$ bits relative to a single prime, and we prove that the *which-factor wall* — the extra information in the ordered type pair — vanishes identically for every finite group whenever the residue is read through the abelianization. All decimal values are certified by exact integer power comparisons.

---

## 1. Introduction

The splitting of rational primes in number fields is one of the oldest themes of algebraic number theory, and cyclotomic fields are its best-understood laboratory. In $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ a prime $p \nmid n$ splits into $\varphi(n)/t$ primes of residue degree $t$, where $t$ is the multiplicative order of $p$ modulo $n$. Cyclotomic rings are also the arithmetic substrate of a large part of modern lattice-based cryptography, where the factorization of $\Phi_n$ modulo a prime governs the Chinese-remainder (number-theoretic transform) decomposition of the ring.

We adopt an information-theoretic viewpoint. Treat a random unramified prime as a random Frobenius class, uniformly distributed over the Galois group (the content of the Chebotarev density theorem, or for cyclotomic fields, Dirichlet's theorem). Then the residue of $p$ and its splitting type become two random variables on a finite probability space, and one can ask: *how many bits of the splitting type does the residue reveal?* Call this the **type channel**.

A sequence of computations for abelian fields of degrees $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9$ — real subfields of cyclotomic fields and full cyclotomic fields — has found in every case that the residue reveals *all* of the type: the mutual information equals the type entropy. We call this **full pinning**. This paper treats the tenth rung, the full cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$, and does more: it proves full pinning for all abelian fields at once, derives the exact degree-ten constants, and settles several numerical questions raised by the experimental record.

### 1.1 Experimental background

The following predictions were made for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ in advance and checked on data:

1. The type $T(p) = \operatorname{ord}_{11}(p)$ takes values in $\{1,2,5,10\}$ with densities $\{1/10, 1/10, 4/10, 4/10\}$; this was observed on $295{,}946$ unramified primes.
2. $I(p \bmod 11;\ T) = H(T) \approx 1.7219$ bits, with the type degenerate on each residue class.
3. On $400$ primes, the factor-degree pattern of $\Phi_{11} \bmod p$ was $[1^{10}]$, $[2^5]$, $[5,5]$ or $[10]$ according as $\operatorname{ord}_{11}(p) = 1, 2, 5, 10$.
4. For semiprimes, the channel $I(N \bmod 11;\ \text{type pair})$ was measured at $1.2002$, against an enumeration value $1.1999$ and an earlier closed-form prediction $1.2027$.

We prove items 1–3 exactly (item 3 for all primes and all conductors), and we resolve item 4: the exact law is $1.20271\ldots$, agreeing with the closed-form prediction to within $3\cdot 10^{-5}$ and strictly exceeding both other figures, which are therefore finite-sample estimates.

### 1.2 Summary of results

- **Theorem A (cyclic Chebotarev densities).** In a cyclic group of order $n$, exactly $\varphi(d)$ elements have order $d$ for each $d \mid n$; hence every cyclic field has type entropy $H(T) = -\sum_{d \mid n}\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\log_2\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}$.
- **Theorem B (abelian full pinning).** For any finite abelian group, any injective residue readout $c$ and any type readout $T$: $I(c;T) = H(T)$, $H(T\mid c) = 0$, and $\log_2|A| - I(c;T) = H(c \mid T)$.
- **Theorem C (degree ten).** $I(p \bmod 11; T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \frac35$, $H(T \mid p \bmod 11) = 0$, $H(p \bmod 11 \mid T) = \frac85$.
- **Theorem D (factor patterns, all conductors).** $\Phi_n \bmod p$ has factor-degree multiset $[t^{\varphi(n)/t}]$, $t = \operatorname{ord}_n(p)$, equal to the cycle type of multiplication by $p$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$.
- **Theorem E (tower).** $H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - \frac85$, the real subfield is fully pinned, $H(T \mid T^+) = 1$, and $H(T) = H_{C_2} + H_{C_5}$.
- **Theorem F (semiprime channel).** $I(N \bmod 11; \{T(p),T(q)\}) = \log_2 5 + \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \frac{47}{25}$.
- **Theorem G (which-factor wall).** For any finite group $G$ and any residue readout with $c(gh) = c(hg)$ — in particular any abelian $G$, or any $G$ read through its abelianization — ordered and unordered type pairs carry identical information about $c(gh)$.
- **Theorem H (attenuation and certified numerics).** $H(T) - I_{\mathrm{semi}} = \frac{32}{25} - \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3$, and $1.7219 < H(T) < 1.72193$, $1.20268 < I_{\mathrm{semi}} < 1.20272$.

---

## 2. Setting and definitions

### 2.1 Frobenius and splitting types

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite Galois extension with group $G$, and let $p$ be a prime unramified in $K$. The Frobenius elements of primes above $p$ form a conjugacy class $\operatorname{Frob}_p \subseteq G$. If $\operatorname{Frob}_p$ has order $t$ then $p$ factors in $K$ as a product of $|G|/t$ distinct primes, each of residue degree $t$.

**Definition 2.1 (Frobenius type).** The *Frobenius type* of $p$ in $K$ is $T(p) = $ the order of $\operatorname{Frob}_p$. More generally a *type readout* is any function $T : G \to \tau$ into a set of labels.

For the cyclotomic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$, the Galois group is canonically $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$, via $\sigma_a : \zeta_n \mapsto \zeta_n^a$, and the Frobenius of a prime $p \nmid n$ is $\sigma_p$, i.e. the residue class $p \bmod n$. Thus $T(p) = \operatorname{ord}_n(p)$.

For the maximal real subfield $K^+ = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n + \zeta_n^{-1})$ the Galois group is $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times / \{\pm 1\}$, and the type $T^+(p)$ is the order of the image of $p$ in that quotient. For $n = 11$ the squaring map $g \mapsto g^2$ has kernel exactly $\{\pm 1\}$ — indeed $g^2 = h^2$ iff $g = \pm h$ — so it identifies the quotient with the subgroup of squares, and $T^+(p) = \operatorname{ord}_{11}(p^2)$.

### 2.2 The uniform-Frobenius model and information quantities

**Definition 2.2 (uniform model).** A *sample* is a finite set $S$ with the uniform probability measure. For the single-prime channel of an abelian field with group $A$, the sample is $S = A$: a random unramified prime is modelled by a uniformly random Frobenius element. For semiprimes $N = pq$ the sample is $A \times A$, the Frobenius classes of $p$ and $q$ being independent and uniform.

By the Chebotarev density theorem, this model describes the natural density of primes exactly.

**Definition 2.3 (entropy and mutual information).** For a readout $f : S \to \alpha$, the probability of a value $a$ is $P(f = a) = |\{w \in S : f(w) = a\}|/|S|$ and
$$H(f) = -\sum_{a} P(f=a)\log_2 P(f=a).$$
For two readouts $f,g$ we write $(f,g)$ for the joint readout $w \mapsto (f(w), g(w))$, and set
$$H(f \mid g) = H(f,g) - H(g), \qquad I(f;g) = H(f) + H(g) - H(f,g).$$

**Definition 2.4 (residue readout, full pinning).** A *residue readout* on a group $G$ is a function $c : G \to \kappa$; for cyclotomic fields we take $c(g) = $ the residue $p \bmod n$ itself, which is injective. The readout $c$ *fully pins* $T$ if $I(c;T) = H(T)$.

Since $I(c;T) = H(T) - H(T \mid c)$, full pinning is equivalent to *per-class degeneracy*: $H(T\mid c) = 0$, i.e. $T$ is constant on each fibre of $c$.

---

## 3. Cyclic fields: densities and closed-form type entropy

**Theorem 3.1 (Chebotarev densities of a cyclic field).** Let $G$ be a cyclic group of order $n$ and $d \mid n$. Then exactly $\varphi(d)$ elements of $G$ have order $d$. Consequently, in a cyclic field of degree $n$, the type $T = \operatorname{ord}$ takes the value $d$ with density $\varphi(d)/n$.

*Proof sketch.* $G$ has a unique subgroup of order $d$, which is cyclic, and the elements of order exactly $d$ are its generators, of which there are $\varphi(d)$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.2 (closed-form type entropy).** For a cyclic Galois group of order $n$,
$$H(T) = -\sum_{d \mid n} \frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\log_2\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Every element order divides $n$, so the values of $T$ lie in the divisor set of $n$; substitute the fibre sizes of Theorem 3.1 into Definition 2.3. $\square$

For $n = 10$, the divisors $1, 2, 5, 10$ have totients $1, 1, 4, 4$. Explicitly, in $(\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$:

| type $d$ | elements of order $d$ | count $=\varphi(d)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $10$ | $1$ |
| $5$ | $3, 4, 5, 9$ | $4$ |
| $10$ | $2, 6, 7, 8$ | $4$ |

---

## 4. The abelian full-pinning law

**Theorem 4.1 (abelian full pinning).** Let $A$ be a finite abelian group, $c : A \to \kappa$ an injective residue readout, and $T : A \to \tau$ any type readout. Then, in the uniform model on $A$,
1. $I(c;T) = H(T)$ (the residue pins the type);
2. $H(T \mid c) = 0$ (per-class degeneracy);
3. $\log_2|A| - I(c;T) = H(c \mid T)$ (the loss equals the residue uncertainty given the type).

*Proof sketch.* The theorem is the abelian specialization of a general *coset law* for an arbitrary finite group $G$ with derived subgroup $G'$: if $c$ is a *coset readout*, i.e. $c(a) = c(b)$ iff $ab^{-1} \in G'$, then $c$ sees exactly the image of Frobenius in the abelianization $G/G'$, and one has $I(c;T) = H(T) - H(T\mid c)$, $\log_2|c(G)| - I(c;T) = H(c\mid T)$, and $I(c;T) = H(T)$ whenever $T$ is constant on $G'$-cosets. For abelian $A$ the derived subgroup is trivial, every injective readout is a coset readout, and every $T$ is constant on the (singleton) cosets. Concretely, $T$ factors through $c$, so the joint readout $(c,T)$ has the same fibres as $c$; thus $H(c,T) = H(c) = \log_2|A|$, which gives all three identities at once. $\square$

**Remark 4.2 (why abelianness is the right hypothesis).** In a non-abelian Galois group, a residue that is a class-field-theoretic invariant (a congruence condition) can only see the image of Frobenius in $G/G'$. Distinct conjugacy classes with different orders may share an abelianization image, in which case $H(T \mid c) > 0$ and pinning fails. Theorem 4.1 shows that in abelian fields there is no such obstruction: *every* splitting statistic is a function of the residue. This explains why the full-pinning prediction succeeded on every abelian rung examined — degrees $2$–$6$, $8$, $9$ and $10$, real subfields and full cyclotomic fields alike — with no exceptions.

---

## 5. Degree ten: exact constants

Let $A = (\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$, let $c(g) = g$ (the residue $p \bmod 11$, represented in $\{1,\dots,10\}$) and $T(g) = \operatorname{ord}(g)$.

**Theorem 5.1 (type entropy at degree ten).** $H(T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35 \approx 1.72193$ bits.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1 the type distribution is $(1,1,4,4)/10$. Hence
$$H(T) = \tfrac{2}{10}\log_2 10 + \tfrac{8}{10}\log_2\tfrac{10}{4} = \log_2 10 - \tfrac{8}{10}\cdot 2 = 1 + \log_2 5 - \tfrac85 = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35. \qquad\square$$

**Theorem 5.2 (full pinning at degree ten).** In the uniform-Frobenius model for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$:
$$I(p \bmod 11;\ T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35,\qquad H(T \mid p \bmod 11) = 0,\qquad H(p \bmod 11 \mid T) = \tfrac85.$$

*Proof.* The residue readout is injective, so Theorem 4.1 applies and gives the first two statements together with $\log_2 10 - I = H(c\mid T)$. Substituting Theorem 5.1, $H(c \mid T) = 1 + \log_2 5 - (\log_2 5 - \frac35) = \frac85$. $\square$

As an independent check, Corollary 3.2 for $n = 10$ reproduces the same value $\log_2 5 - \frac35$.

The interpretation of $8/5$ is direct: of the $\log_2 10 \approx 3.3219$ bits in the residue, $1.7219$ bits determine the splitting type, and the remaining $1.6$ bits distinguish residues sharing the same type (for example $3, 4, 5, 9$, all of type $5$). The type is a lossy summary of the residue; never the converse.

---

## 6. Factor patterns of cyclotomic polynomials, for every conductor

The experimental record checked factor patterns of $\Phi_{11}$ on $400$ primes. We replace this by a theorem for all primes and all conductors.

**Theorem 6.1 (factor-degree law).** Let $n \ge 1$ and $p$ a prime with $p \nmid n$, and let $t = \operatorname{ord}_n(p)$. Every monic irreducible factor of $\Phi_n$ in $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ has degree $t$. Consequently the multiset of degrees of irreducible factors is
$$[\underbrace{t, t, \dots, t}_{\varphi(n)/t}].$$

*Proof sketch.* Since $p \nmid n$, $\Phi_n$ is separable over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and its roots are the primitive $n$-th roots of unity in $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. A primitive $n$-th root $\eta$ lies in $\mathbb{F}_{p^k}$ iff $n \mid p^k - 1$, i.e. iff $t \mid k$; so $[\mathbb{F}_p(\eta):\mathbb{F}_p] = t$ and the minimal polynomial of every root has degree $t$. Since $\deg \Phi_n = \varphi(n)$ is the sum of the factor degrees, there are $\varphi(n)/t$ factors. $\square$

**Lemma 6.2 (group-side mirror).** Let $G$ be a finite group and $g \in G$. The permutation $x \mapsto gx$ of $G$ has all cycles of length $\operatorname{ord}(g)$, and the number of cycles is the index $[G : \langle g\rangle] = |G|/\operatorname{ord}(g)$.

*Proof sketch.* The cycles are the right cosets $\langle g\rangle x$, each of size $\operatorname{ord}(g)$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (factor pattern $=$ orbit pattern).** For $p \nmid n$, the factor-degree multiset of $\Phi_n$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ equals the cycle type of multiplication by the Frobenius class $p \bmod n$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$: $[\langle p\rangle$-index copies of the period of $x \mapsto px]$.

*Proof.* Combine Theorem 6.1 and Lemma 6.2 with $|(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times| = \varphi(n)$. $\square$

**Corollary 6.4 (polynomial-level full pinning).** If $p, q \nmid n$ are primes with $p \equiv q \pmod n$, then $\Phi_n$ has the same factor-degree pattern over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

**Corollary 6.5 (the four degree-ten patterns).** For every prime $p \ne 11$, the factor pattern of $\Phi_{11}$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ is one of $[1^{10}]$, $[2^5]$, $[5,5]$, $[10]$, according as $\operatorname{ord}_{11}(p) = 1, 2, 5, 10$, and it is determined by $p \bmod 11$ alone as $[\operatorname{ord}(p)^{10/\operatorname{ord}(p)}]$. Witnesses: $p = 23 \equiv 1$ gives $[1^{10}]$; $p = 43 \equiv -1$ gives $[2^5]$; $p = 3$ (order $5$) gives $[5,5]$; $p = 2$ (a primitive root modulo $11$) gives $[10]$, so $\Phi_{11}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

**Remark 6.6 (a computational pitfall).** In the original 400-prime check, a first comparison reported $400/400$ mismatches while every pattern was in fact correct: the predicted pattern had been wrapped in one more layer of tuple than the computed one. A related pitfall is to index a lookup table by residue where it should be indexed by type. Theorem 6.3 makes the correct comparison canonical: both sides are multisets of positive integers summing to $\varphi(n)$.

---

## 7. The tower $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+ \subset \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$

### 7.1 Additivity of entropy for independent readouts

**Lemma 7.1.** Let $S_1, S_2$ be nonempty finite samples and $f : S_1 \to \alpha$, $g : S_2 \to \beta$. On the product sample $S_1 \times S_2$ the readout $(x,y) \mapsto (f(x), g(y))$ has entropy $H(f) + H(g)$.

*Proof sketch.* Fibres of the product readout are products of fibres, so probabilities multiply and $-\log_2$ turns products into sums. $\square$

### 7.2 The CRT splitting

$(\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times \cong C_{10} \cong C_2 \times C_5$, with $C_2 = \{\pm 1\} = \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+)$ and $C_5$ the subgroup of squares $\{1, 3, 4, 5, 9\} = \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-11}))$. Under this decomposition the order of an element is the product of the orders of its components, and the product map is injective on pairs of coprime divisors $(d_2, d_5) \in \{1,2\}\times\{1,5\}$.

**Theorem 7.2 (CRT additivity at degree ten).** $H(T) = H_{C_2}(\operatorname{ord}) + H_{C_5}(\operatorname{ord})$, with $H_{C_2}(\operatorname{ord}) = 1$ and $H_{C_5}(\operatorname{ord}) = \log_2 5 - \frac85$.

*Proof sketch.* Transport the uniform measure along the isomorphism $C_{10} \to C_2 \times C_5$; $T$ becomes the product of the component orders, which by injectivity carries the same information as the pair of component orders; apply Lemma 7.1. The component values: in $C_2$ the orders $1,2$ are equiprobable (1 bit); in $C_5$ the orders $1,5$ have probabilities $1/5, 4/5$, giving $\frac15\log_2 5 + \frac45\log_2\frac54 = \log_2 5 - \frac85$. $\square$

### 7.3 The real quintic subfield and the tower bit

**Theorem 7.3 (real subfield).** In the degree-five real subfield $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+$, the type $T^+$ takes value $1$ on $\{\pm1\}$ and $5$ elsewhere, so
$$H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac85 \approx 0.72193,$$
and the same residue $p \bmod 11$ fully pins it: $I(p \bmod 11; T^+) = H(T^+)$.

*Proof.* Distribution $(2, 8)/10$; full pinning by Theorem 4.1. $\square$

**Theorem 7.4 (the tower bit).** $H(T \mid T^+) = 1 = \log_2[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11}) : \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+]$. Equivalently, $H(T) = 1 + H(T^+)$, and $H(T^+) = H_{C_5}(\operatorname{ord})$.

*Proof.* The joint readout $(T^+, T)$ takes the values $(1,1), (1,2), (5,5), (5,10)$ with counts $1, 1, 4, 4$, so $H(T^+,T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \frac35$, and $H(T\mid T^+) = (\log_2 5 - \frac35) - (\log_2 5 - \frac85) = 1$. $\square$

---

## 8. The semiprime channel

Let $N = pq$ with $p, q \ne 11$ having independent uniform Frobenius classes $(g, h) \in A \times A$. Then $N \bmod 11 = gh$. Define the readouts
$$\nu(g,h) = gh, \qquad \pi(g,h) = \{T(g), T(h)\}\ (\text{unordered}),\qquad \omega(g,h) = (T(g), T(h))\ (\text{ordered}).$$

**Theorem 8.1 (semiprime channel, exact).**
$$I\big(N \bmod 11;\ \{T(p),T(q)\}\big) = \log_2 5 + \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \tfrac{47}{25} \approx 1.2027101.$$

*Proof sketch.* All three entropies are computed from exact fibre counts on the $100$-element sample.

- $\nu$ is uniform on $10$ residues: $H(\nu) = \log_2 10 = 1 + \log_2 5$.
- $\pi$ takes the ten unordered values $\{1,1\},\{1,2\},\{1,5\},\{1,10\},\{2,2\},\{2,5\},\{2,10\},\{5,5\},\{5,10\},\{10,10\}$ with counts $1,2,8,8,1,8,8,16,32,16$, giving $H(\pi) = 2\log_2 5 - \frac{93}{50}$.
- The joint readout $(\nu,\pi)$ has $34$ nonempty cells with counts in $\{1,2,3,4,6,8\}$ (for instance, $\nu = 1$ splits as $\{1,1\}:1$, $\{2,2\}:1$, $\{5,5\}:4$, $\{10,10\}:4$; $\nu = 10$ splits as $\{1,2\}:2$, $\{5,10\}:8$; each quadratic-residue class $\nu \in \{3,4,5,9\}$ splits as $\{1,5\}:2$, $\{2,10\}:2$, $\{5,5\}:3$, $\{10,10\}:3$; each non-residue class $\nu \in\{2,6,7,8\}$ splits as $\{1,10\}:2$, $\{2,5\}:2$, $\{5,10\}:6$). Summing, $H(\nu,\pi) = 2\log_2 5 + \frac{51}{50} - \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3$.

Then $I = H(\nu) + H(\pi) - H(\nu,\pi) = \log_2 5 + \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \frac{47}{25}$. $\square$

The terms in $\log_2 3$ arise solely from the cells of size $3$ and $6$, which occur because each square class $\nu$ of order $5$ is hit by exactly three ordered pairs of type $(5,5)$ and three of type $(10,10)$.

**Theorem 8.2 (ordered channel).** $H(\omega) = 2\log_2 5 - \frac65 = 2H(T)$, $H(\nu,\omega) = 2\log_2 5 + \frac{42}{25} - \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3$, and
$$I(N \bmod 11;\ (T(p),T(q))) = \log_2 5 + \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \tfrac{47}{25}.$$
In particular the *which-factor wall* $I(\nu;\omega) - I(\nu;\pi)$ vanishes at degree ten.

This was obtained by a direct $56$-cell count; Section 9 proves it structurally for all groups.

---

## 9. The which-factor wall vanishes structurally

**Lemma 9.1 (entropy as average surprisal).** $H(f) = \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{w \in S} -\log_2 P(f = f(w))$.

For a pair $o = (o_1, o_2)$ in a linearly ordered set, write $\operatorname{sym}(o) = (\min, \max)$; then $\operatorname{sym}(o) = \operatorname{sym}(o')$ iff $o' = o$ or $o' = o^{\mathrm{swap}}$.

**Lemma 9.2 (swap-symmetric pairs lose exactly the off-diagonal mass).** Let $\sigma$ be an involution of a finite sample $S$, let $Y$ be a readout with $Y\circ\sigma = Y$ and $O = (O_1, O_2)$ a pair readout with $O\circ\sigma = O^{\mathrm{swap}}$. Then
$$H(Y, O) = H\big(Y, \operatorname{sym} O\big) + P(O_1 \ne O_2).$$

*Proof sketch.* Use Lemma 9.1 pointwise. If $O_1(w) = O_2(w)$, the fibres of $(Y,O)$ and $(Y, \operatorname{sym}O)$ through $w$ coincide. If $O_1(w) \ne O_2(w)$, the fibre of $(Y,\operatorname{sym} O)$ through $w$ is the disjoint union of the $(Y,O)$-fibres through $w$ and through $\sigma(w)$, which $\sigma$ puts in bijection; so its probability is exactly twice as large and the surprisal drops by exactly one bit. Averaging gives $P(O_1 \ne O_2)$. $\square$

**Theorem 9.3 (which-factor wall, swap-invariant readouts).** Let $G$ be a group, $S \subseteq G$ finite, $c : G \to \kappa$ a readout with $c(gh) = c(hg)$ for all $g,h \in S$, and $T : G \to \tau$ a type readout into a linearly ordered set. On the sample $S\times S$,
$$I\big(c(gh);\ (T g, T h)\big) = I\big(c(gh);\ \{T g, T h\}\big).$$

*Proof.* Take $\sigma(g,h) = (h,g)$. Apply Lemma 9.2 once with $Y = c(gh)$ and once with $Y$ constant. Both corrections equal $P(Tg \ne Th)$, so in $I(Y;O) = H(Y) + H(O) - H(Y,O)$ they cancel. $\square$

**Corollary 9.4 (abelianization).** Let $G$ be any finite group with derived subgroup $G'$, and let $c$ be a coset readout of $G'$ ($c(a) = c(b)$ iff $ab^{-1} \in G'$). Then the which-factor wall vanishes for every type readout. In particular it vanishes for every finite abelian group and every readout whatsoever.

*Proof.* $(gh)(hg)^{-1} = ghg^{-1}h^{-1} = [g,h] \in G'$, so $c(gh) = c(hg)$; apply Theorem 9.3. $\square$

Applied to $A = (\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$ this re-derives Theorem 8.2 without any cell count. Applied to the non-abelian groups $D_4$ (order $8$, symmetries of the square) and $A_4$ (order $12$, rotations of the tetrahedron) with their abelianization readouts, it explains why previously computed which-factor walls for these groups were exactly zero.

**Remark 9.5 (the reported wall of $0.0005$).** The figure $0.0005$ was the difference between two *estimates* ($1.2002$ measured and $1.1999$ enumerated) of the same quantity. By Theorem 9.3 the genuine which-factor wall is identically zero, and by Theorem 8.1 both estimates sit below the exact value.

---

## 10. Attenuation and certified numerics

**Theorem 10.1 (semiprime attenuation).** At degree ten the semiprime channel is strictly weaker than the single-prime channel:
$$H(T) - I\big(N \bmod 11; \{T(p),T(q)\}\big) = \tfrac{32}{25} - \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 \approx 0.51922 > 0.$$

*Proof.* Subtract Theorem 8.1 from Theorem 5.1; positivity follows from $\log_2 3 < 8/3$. $\square$

**Lemma 10.2 (enclosures from integer powers).** For positive integers $a, m, n$: if $2^m < a^n$ then $m/n < \log_2 a$, and if $a^n < 2^m$ then $\log_2 a < m/n$. The exact integer inequalities
$$2^{23219} < 5^{10000},\quad 5^{100000} < 2^{232193},\quad 2^{158496} < 3^{100000},\quad 3^{100000} < 2^{158497}$$
give
$$2.3219 < \log_2 5 < 2.32193,\qquad 1.58496 < \log_2 3 < 1.58497.$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply the strictly increasing function $\log_2$ and divide by $n$. $\square$

**Theorem 10.3 (certified values).**
1. $1.7219 < I(p \bmod 11; T) = H(T) < 1.72193$.
2. $1.20268 < I_{\mathrm{semi}} < 1.20272$; hence $|I_{\mathrm{semi}} - 1.2027| < 3\cdot 10^{-5}$ and $I_{\mathrm{semi}} > 1.2002 > 1.1999$.

*Proof.* Insert Lemma 10.2 into the closed forms of Theorems 5.1 and 8.1; these are linear in $\log_2 5$ and $\log_2 3$ with explicit rational coefficients. $\square$

Thus the earlier closed-form prediction $1.2027$ *is* the law, and the enumeration value $1.1999$ is not.

---

## 11. Algorithms

**Algorithm 1 (exact type channel of a finite abelian group).** Input: a finite group given by its multiplication table, readouts $c$ and $T$. (i) Tabulate fibre counts of $c$, $T$ and $(c,T)$; (ii) compute entropies from counts. Cost $O(|G|)$ after the readouts are evaluated. For $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$, computing all orders costs $O(\varphi(n)\cdot \lambda(n))$ naively, or $O(\varphi(n)\,\omega(\varphi(n))\log n)$ by testing $g^{\varphi(n)/r}$ for primes $r \mid \varphi(n)$. For the semiprime channel the sample is $G\times G$, cost $O(|G|^2)$.

**Algorithm 2 (factor pattern by distinct-degree factorization).** Input: prime $p \nmid n$. Set $f = \Phi_n \bmod p$, $h = x$. For $d = 1, 2, \dots$: replace $h \leftarrow h^p \bmod f$; $g = \gcd(f, h - x)$; record $\deg g / d$ factors of degree $d$; set $f \leftarrow f/g$; stop when $2d > \deg f$, recording the remaining $f$ as one factor if non-constant. This computes the pattern without reference to $\operatorname{ord}_n(p)$, giving an independent check of Theorem 6.1; its cost is $O(\varphi(n)^3\log p)$ field operations with schoolbook arithmetic. By Theorem 6.1 it can be replaced by a single order computation.

**Algorithm 3 (certified enclosure of $\log_2 a$).** To certify $m/n < \log_2 a < m'/n'$, compare the exact integers $2^m$ vs $a^n$ and $a^{n'}$ vs $2^{m'}$. With $n = 10^5$ this costs a few multiplications of integers with $\approx 2\cdot 10^5$ bits.

---

## 12. Discussion

**What the tenth rung establishes.** Every prediction formulated in advance for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ is now a theorem in the uniform-Frobenius model: the densities $(1,1,4,4)/10$; full pinning at $\log_2 5 - \frac35$; per-class degeneracy; the residual $8/5$ bits. The factor-pattern check has been upgraded from $400$ primes to all primes and all conductors. The semiprime law has been corrected from the enumeration value $1.1999$ to the exact $1.20271$, matching the earlier closed form. The which-factor wall has been shown to vanish for structural reasons.

**Scope of full pinning.** Theorem 4.1 shows that full pinning is not a numerical coincidence accumulating rung by rung: for an abelian field, the residue modulo the conductor is the Frobenius, so every function of Frobenius — in particular every splitting statistic — is pinned. The interesting quantity is therefore not $I(c;T)$, which always equals $H(T)$, but the loss $H(c\mid T) = \log_2|A| - H(T)$, which measures how coarse the splitting type is relative to the full Frobenius. At degree ten it is $8/5$ bits; in the real quintic subfield it is $\log_2 5 - H(T^+) = 8/5$ bits as well.

**Cryptographic reading.** For cyclotomic rings $\mathbb{Z}[x]/\Phi_n$ used in lattice-based cryptography, Theorem 6.3 says the CRT decomposition of $\mathbb{F}_p[x]/\Phi_n$ is into $\varphi(n)/t$ copies of $\mathbb{F}_{p^t}$, determined entirely by $p \bmod n$. The semiprime results quantify a different phenomenon: a residue of a product $N = pq$ reveals strictly less about the splitting behaviour of the factors than a residue of a single prime does — at degree ten exactly $0.519$ bits less — and the attenuation is a consequence of multiplicative mixing of the two Frobenius classes.

**Limitations.** All statements concern the uniform-Frobenius model; their relation to finite prime counts is through the Chebotarev density theorem, and finite-sample estimates (such as $1.2002$ and $1.1999$) deviate from the law by sampling error. A further statistic reported in the experimental record (a projection value of $0.0586$ for an "$\mathrm{Is}(10)$" construction) is not treated here because its definition could not be reconstructed unambiguously.

---

## 13. Future work

1. **The 2-adic tower-gap law (conjecture).** For an odd prime $p$, $H(T) - H(T^+) = 2^{1 - v_2(p-1)}$ for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ and its maximal real subfield. The data give $1$ bit when $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ (as for $p = 11$, Theorem 7.4) and $1/2$ when $p \equiv 5 \pmod 8$. Writing $C_{p-1} = C_{2^k}\times C_{\mathrm{odd}}$, the odd part should cancel by CRT additivity, leaving $H(C_{2^k}) - H(C_{2^{k-1}}) = 2^{1-k}$.
2. **CRT additivity of cyclotomic type entropy (conjecture).** For coprime $m,n$, $H_{C_{mn}}(\operatorname{ord}) = H_{C_m}(\operatorname{ord}) + H_{C_n}(\operatorname{ord})$, with strict failure for non-coprime pairs (the data show losses of $0.75$ and $0.816$ bits for $(2,4)$ and $(3,9)$). Theorem 7.2 is the case $(m,n) = (2,5)$.
3. **Strict semiprime attenuation for every prime conductor $\ell \ge 5$ (conjecture).** $I(N \bmod \ell; \{T(p),T(q)\}) < H(T_\ell)$, with attenuation growing along primes for which $\ell - 1$ has many divisors. Theorem 10.1 is the first nontrivial calibration point, and Theorem 9.3 reduces the problem to the unordered pair.
4. **Real-subfield polynomial pinning (conjecture).** The minimal polynomial of $2\cos(2\pi/n)$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ factors as $\varphi(n)/(2t^+)$ irreducibles of degree $t^+$, where $t^+$ is the order of $p$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times/\{\pm1\}$ — the real-subfield analogue of Theorem 6.1.
5. **Non-abelian rungs.** Quantify the failure of pinning, $H(T\mid c) > 0$, for coset readouts of non-abelian Galois groups, where the residue sees only the abelianization.

def mult_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Multiplicative order of a modulo n (gcd(a, n) = 1 assumed)."""
    a %= n
    k, x = 1, a
    while x != 1:
        x = (x * a) % n
        k += 1
    return k


def totient(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if math.gcd(k, n) == 1)


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return [d for d in range(1, n + 1) if n % d == 0]

demos.name: The Which-Factor Wall Across Abelian and Non-Abelian Groups
demos.description: For a finite group G and uniformly random pairs (g, h), compares the mutual information between a residue c(gh) and the ordered type pair (T g, T h) with that for the unordered pair {T g, T h}. It confirms the swap lemma H(Y,O) − H(Y,sym O) = P(O₁ ≠ O₂) and the vanishing wall for (ℤ/11)ˣ (both 1.202710 bits), for S₃ read through its sign character, and for A₄ read through A₄/V₄ ≅ ℤ/3; it then exhibits a genuine nonzero wall (≈ 0.2495 bits) on S₃ when the residue distinguishes gh from hg and the type is not conjugation-invariant, showing that the hypotheses of the theorem matter.
demos.code:
"""The which-factor wall: ordered vs unordered type pairs.

For a finite group G, sample (g, h) uniformly from G x G, observe a residue c(gh), and compare
I(c(gh); (T g, T h)) with I(c(gh); {T g, T h}).  The theorem: if c(gh) = c(hg) always (true in
every abelian group, and in every group when c reads only the coset of the derived subgroup),
the two are EQUAL.  When c can distinguish gh from hg (and the type is not conjugation
invariant), a genuine wall can appear.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from collections import Counter
from typing import Callable, Hashable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


def entropy(values: Sequence[Hashable]) -> float:
    c = Counter(values)
    n = len(values)
    return -sum(v / n * math.log2(v / n) for v in c.values())


def mutual_info(xs: Sequence[Hashable], ys: Sequence[Hashable]) -> float:
    return entropy(xs) + entropy(ys) - entropy(list(zip(xs, ys)))


def wall(G: List[Perm], mul: Callable[[Perm, Perm], Perm],
         c: Callable[[Perm], Hashable], T: Callable[[Perm], int]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    Y = [c(mul(g, h)) for g in G for h in G]
    ordered = [(T(g), T(h)) for g in G for h in G]
    unordered = [tuple(sorted(o)) for o in ordered]
    io, iu = mutual_info(Y, ordered), mutual_info(Y, unordered)
    # swap lemma: H(Y,O) - H(Y,sym O) = P(O1 != O2)
    p_off = sum(1 for o in ordered if o[0] != o[1]) / len(ordered)
    lemma_gap = entropy(list(zip(Y, ordered))) - entropy(list(zip(Y, unordered)))
    swap_inv = all(c(mul(g, h)) == c(mul(h, g)) for g in G for h in G)
    if swap_inv:  # the swap lemma applies exactly
        assert abs(lemma_gap - p_off) < 1e-9
    return io, iu, io - iu


def compose(a: Perm, b: Perm) -> Perm:
    return tuple(a[b[i]] for i in range(len(a)))


def perm_order(a: Perm) -> int:
    e = tuple(range(len(a)))
    x, k = a, 1
    while x != e:
        x, k = compose(a, x), k + 1
    return k


def sign(a: Perm) -> int:
    s = 1
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
            if a[i] > a[j]:
                s = -s
    return s


def main() -> None:
    # cyclic group (Z/11)^x, residue readout
    U = [(g,) for g in range(1, 11)]
    mul11 = lambda a, b: ((a[0] * b[0]) % 11,)
    T11 = lambda a: next(k for k in range(1, 11) if pow(a[0], k, 11) == 1)
    io, iu, w = wall(U, mul11, lambda a: a, T11)
    print(f"(Z/11)^x, residue readout      : ordered {io:.6f}  unordered {iu:.6f}  wall {w:+.1e}")

    S3 = list(itertools.permutations(range(3)))
    io, iu, w = wall(S3, compose, sign, perm_order)
    print(f"S3, abelianization (sign)      : ordered {io:.6f}  unordered {iu:.6f}  wall {w:+.1e}")
    # A readout that CAN tell gh from hg, with a type that is not a class function:
    # T(g) = g(0).  Here the hypothesis of the theorem fails and a genuine wall appears.
    io, iu, w = wall(S3, compose, lambda a: a, lambda a: a[0])
    print(f"S3, c(gh) = gh, T(g) = g(0)    : ordered {io:.6f}  unordered {iu:.6f}  wall {w:+.6f}")

    S4 = list(itertools.permutations(range(4)))
    A4 = [a for a in S4 if sign(a) == 1]
    # abelianization of A4 is Z/3: read the coset of the Klein four-group V4
    V4 = {a for a in A4 if perm_order(a) in (1, 2)}
    reps: List[Perm] = []
    for a in A4:
        if not any(compose(a, tuple(sorted(range(4), key=lambda i: r[i]))) in V4 for r in reps):
            reps.append(a)
    def coset(a: Perm) -> int:
        for k, r in enumerate(reps):
            rinv = tuple(sorted(range(4), key=lambda i: r[i]))
            if compose(a, rinv) in V4:
                return k
        raise ValueError
    io, iu, w = wall(A4, compose, coset, perm_order)
    print(f"A4, abelianization (A4/V4)     : ordered {io:.6f}  unordered {iu:.6f}  wall {w:+.1e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Exact Type-Channel Computation for Cyclotomic Fields in the Uniform-Frobenius Model
algorithms.description: Given a conductor n, enumerates the Galois group (ℤ/n)ˣ of Q(ζₙ), computes the Frobenius type T(g) = ord(g) of every element, and tabulates fibre counts of the residue readout, of T, and of the joint readout. Entropies are computed exactly from these counts, yielding the Chebotarev densities φ(d)/φ(n) (when the group is cyclic), the type entropy H(T), the mutual information I(c;T), the per-class conditional entropy H(T|c) (always 0, by the abelian full-pinning law) and the loss H(c|T) = log₂φ(n) − H(T). At n = 11 it returns H(T) = log₂5 − 3/5 and loss 8/5. Complexity: O(φ(n)·λ(n)) multiplications for the naive order computation (λ the Carmichael function) and O(φ(n)) for the counting; the semiprime variant runs over (ℤ/n)ˣ × (ℤ/n)ˣ in O(φ(n)²).
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: conductor n ≥ 3
1. U ← { a ∈ [1, n−1] : gcd(a, n) = 1 }
2. FOR each g ∈ U: T[g] ← least k ≥ 1 with g^k ≡ 1 (mod n)
3. typeCounts ← histogram of T over U
4. jointCounts ← histogram of (g, T[g]) over U      // residue readout is injective
5. H_T ← −Σ_d (typeCounts[d]/|U|) log₂(typeCounts[d]/|U|)
6. H_c ← log₂|U|;  H_cT ← entropy(jointCounts)
7. I ← H_c + H_T − H_cT;  H(T|c) ← H_cT − H_c;  H(c|T) ← H_cT − H_T
8. RETURN densities typeCounts/|U|, H_T, I, H(T|c), H(c|T)
algorithms.code:
"""Exact type channel of a cyclotomic field Q(zeta_n) in the uniform-Frobenius model."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List


def units(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return [a for a in range(1, n) if math.gcd(a, n) == 1]


def mult_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    x, k = a % n, 1
    while x != 1:
        x, k = (x * a) % n, k + 1
    return k


def entropy_from_counts(counts: Dict[object, int]) -> float:
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return -sum(c / total * math.log2(c / total) for c in counts.values() if c)


def type_channel(n: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Return densities, H(T), I(residue;T), H(T|residue) and the loss H(residue|T)."""
    U = units(n)
    T = {g: mult_order(g, n) for g in U}
    type_counts = Counter(T.values())
    joint_counts = Counter((g, T[g]) for g in U)          # residue is injective
    H_T = entropy_from_counts(type_counts)
    H_c = math.log2(len(U))
    H_joint = entropy_from_counts(joint_counts)
    return {
        "densities": {d: Fraction(c, len(U)) for d, c in sorted(type_counts.items())},
        "H(T)": H_T,
        "I(c;T)": H_c + H_T - H_joint,
        "H(T|c)": H_joint - H_c,
        "H(c|T)": H_joint - H_T,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for n in (5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 16):
        r = type_channel(n)
        print(n, r["densities"], f"H(T)={r['H(T)']:.5f}", f"I={r['I(c;T)']:.5f}",
              f"H(T|c)={r['H(T|c)']:.1e}", f"loss={r['H(c|T)']:.5f}")

algorithms.name: Distinct-Degree Factorization of Φₙ over 𝔽_p and the Orbit-Pattern Cross-Check
algorithms.description: Computes the multiset of degrees of the irreducible factors of the cyclotomic polynomial Φₙ modulo a prime p ∤ n without using the order of p, by distinct-degree factorization: at step d, the polynomial gcd(f, x^(p^d) − x) collects exactly the product of the irreducible factors of degree d. The result is compared with the cycle type of the permutation x ↦ px of (ℤ/n)ˣ, which by the factor-pattern theorem must agree: both equal φ(n)/t copies of t = ordₙ(p). Φₙ itself is generated over ℤ from x^n − 1 = ∏_{d|n} Φ_d. Complexity: O(φ(n)³ log p) field operations with schoolbook polynomial arithmetic; the orbit pattern costs O(φ(n)).
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: n, prime p with p ∤ n
1. f ← Φₙ mod p;  h ← x;  d ← 0;  pattern ← []
2. WHILE deg f > 0:
3.     d ← d + 1
4.     IF 2d > deg f: append deg f to pattern; BREAK
5.     h ← h^p mod f                       // h = x^(p^d) mod f
6.     g ← gcd(f, h − x)
7.     IF deg g > 0: append d, (deg g / d) times; f ← f / g; h ← h mod f
8. orbit ← cycle lengths of a ↦ p·a on (ℤ/n)ˣ
9. ASSERT sorted(pattern) = sorted(orbit) = [t]^(φ(n)/t), t = ordₙ(p)
10. RETURN pattern

algorithms.name: Certified Rational Enclosures of Binary Logarithms by Exact Integer Power Comparison
algorithms.description: Certifies decimal values of the closed forms, which are linear in log₂5 and log₂3 with rational coefficients. For an integer a ≥ 2 that is not a power of two and a precision parameter n, the exponent m = bitlength(aⁿ) − 1 satisfies 2^m < aⁿ < 2^(m+1), whence m/n < log₂a < (m+1)/n because log₂ is strictly increasing. Substituting the enclosures for log₂5 and log₂3 into H(T) = log₂5 − 3/5, I_semi = log₂5 + (12/25)log₂3 − 47/25 and the attenuation 32/25 − (12/25)log₂3 gives rigorous intervals, e.g. 1.7219 < H(T) < 1.72193 and |I_semi − 1.2027| < 3·10⁻⁵. Complexity: one exponentiation of an integer with about n·log₂a bits, i.e. O(M(n) log n) with M the multiplication cost.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: integer a ≥ 2 (not a power of 2), precision n
1. A ← a^n (exact big integer)
2. m ← bitlength(A) − 1           // 2^m < A < 2^(m+1)
3. RETURN (m/n, (m+1)/n) as an enclosure of log₂ a
APPLICATION:
4. (l5, u5) ← enclosure(5, 10^5);  (l3, u3) ← enclosure(3, 10^5)
5. H_T ∈ [l5 − 3/5, u5 − 3/5]
6. I_semi ∈ [l5 + (12/25) l3 − 47/25, u5 + (12/25) u3 − 47/25]
7. ASSERT 1.7219 < H_T < 1.72193 and |I_semi − 1.2027| < 3·10⁻⁵
algorithms.code:
"""Certified rational enclosures of log2(a) from exact integer power comparisons,
and the resulting certified intervals for the degree-ten channel values."""
from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Tuple


def log2_enclosure(a: int, n: int) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Return (m/n, (m+1)/n) with 2^m <= a^n < 2^(m+1); strict on the left unless a is a power of 2."""
    m = (a ** n).bit_length() - 1
    assert 2 ** m <= a ** n < 2 ** (m + 1)
    return Fraction(m, n), Fraction(m + 1, n)


def certified_degree_ten(n: int = 100_000) -> None:
    lo5, hi5 = log2_enclosure(5, n)
    lo3, hi3 = log2_enclosure(3, n)
    HT = (lo5 - Fraction(3, 5), hi5 - Fraction(3, 5))
    Is = (lo5 + Fraction(12, 25) * lo3 - Fraction(47, 25), hi5 + Fraction(12, 25) * hi3 - Fraction(47, 25))
    At = (Fraction(32, 25) - Fraction(12, 25) * hi3, Fraction(32, 25) - Fraction(12, 25) * lo3)
    print(f"log2 5 in [{float(lo5):.7f}, {float(hi5):.7f}]")
    print(f"log2 3 in [{float(lo3):.7f}, {float(hi3):.7f}]")
    print(f"H(T) = I(p mod 11;T)      in [{float(HT[0]):.7f}, {float(HT[1]):.7f}]")
    print(f"I(N mod 11;{{T(p),T(q)}}) in [{float(Is[0]):.7f}, {float(Is[1]):.7f}]")
    print(f"attenuation               in [{float(At[0]):.7f}, {float(At[1]):.7f}]")
    assert Fraction(17219, 10000) < HT[0] and HT[1] <= Fraction(172193, 100000)  # true value is strictly below hi
    assert abs(Is[0] - Fraction(12027, 10000)) < Fraction(3, 100000) and Is[0] > Fraction(12002, 10000)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    certified_degree_ten()

"""Chebotarev densities of Frobenius types in Q(zeta_11): theory vs actual primes,
together with the information budget of the residue p mod 11."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def mult_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    x, k = a % n, 1
    while x != 1:
        x, k = (x * a) % n, k + 1
    return k


def main() -> None:
    types = [1, 2, 5, 10]
    theory = [0.1, 0.1, 0.4, 0.4]
    ps = [p for p in primes_up_to(4_000_000) if p != 11]
    emp = Counter(mult_order(p, 11) for p in ps)
    empirical = [emp[t] / len(ps) for t in types]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6))
    xs = range(len(types))
    ax1.bar([x - 0.18 for x in xs], theory, width=0.36, label=r"Chebotarev $\varphi(d)/10$", color="#4c72b0")
    ax1.bar([x + 0.18 for x in xs], empirical, width=0.36, label=f"{len(ps):,} primes < 4e6", color="#dd8452")

    ax1.set_xticklabels([r"$[1^{10}]$" + "\nsplit", r"$[2^5]$", r"$[5,5]$", r"$[10]$" + "\ninert"])
    ax1.set_ylabel("density")
    ax1.set_title(r"Frobenius type $T(p)=\mathrm{ord}_{11}(p)$")
    ax1.legend()

    HT = math.log2(5) - 0.6
    loss = 1.6
    ax2.barh([0], [HT], color="#55a868", label=r"$I(p \bmod 11;T)=H(T)=\log_2 5-3/5$")
    ax2.barh([0], [loss], left=[HT], color="#c44e52", label=r"$H(p \bmod 11\mid T)=8/5$")
    ax2.barh([1], [HT - 1], color="#8172b2", label=r"real subfield $H(T^+)=\log_2 5-8/5$")

Right: the single-prime type entropy H(T_ℓ) versus the exact semiprime channel I(N mod ℓ; {T(p),T(q)}), with the attenuation shaded and the degree-ten values 1.72193 and 1.20271 marked.
visualizations.code:
"""Across prime conductors l: single-prime type entropy H(T_l), the real-subfield entropy
H(T_l^+), the tower gap H - H^+ (compared with the conjectured 2^{1 - v_2(l-1)}), and the
exact semiprime channel I(N mod l ; {T(p),T(q)}) with its attenuation."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from typing import Callable, Dict, Hashable, List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def mult_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    x, k = a % n, 1
    while x != 1:
        x, k = (x * a) % n, k + 1
    return k


def entropy(values: Sequence[Hashable]) -> float:
    c = Counter(values)
    n = len(values)
    return -sum(v / n * math.log2(v / n) for v in c.values())


def v2(m: int) -> int:
    k = 0
    while m % 2 == 0:
        m //= 2
        k += 1
    return k


def stats(l: int) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    U = list(range(1, l))
    T = {g: mult_order(g, l) for g in U}
    Tp = {g: mult_order(g * g, l) for g in U}
    HT = entropy([T[g] for g in U])
    HTp = entropy([Tp[g] for g in U])
    N = [(g * h) % l for g in U for h in U]
    P = [tuple(sorted((T[g], T[h]))) for g in U for h in U]
    I = entropy(N) + entropy(P) - entropy(list(zip(N, P)))
    return HT, HTp, I


def main() -> None:
    ells = [l for l in range(5, 140) if all(l % d for d in range(2, int(l ** 0.5) + 1))]
    data = [stats(l) for l in ells]
    HT = [d[0] for d in data]
    HTp = [d[1] for d in data]
    I = [d[2] for d in data]
    fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
    a1.plot(ells, [h - hp for h, hp in zip(HT, HTp)], "o", label=r"$H(T)-H(T^+)$ (computed)")
    a1.plot(ells, [2 ** (1 - v2(l - 1)) for l in ells], "x", color="k", label=r"conjecture $2^{1-v_2(\ell-1)}$")
    a1.axvline(11, color="gray", ls=":")
    a1.set_xlabel(r"prime conductor $\ell$")
    a1.set_ylabel("bits")
    a1.set_title("Tower gap between $\\mathbb{Q}(\\zeta_\\ell)$ and its real subfield")
    a1.legend()
    a2.plot(ells, HT, "o-", label=r"single prime $H(T_\ell)$")
    a2.plot(ells, I, "s-", label=r"semiprime $I(N \bmod \ell;\{T(p),T(q)\})$")
    a2.fill_between(ells, I, HT, alpha=0.2, label="attenuation")
    a2.annotate("degree ten: 1.72193 vs 1.20271", (11, 1.2027), (30, 0.8), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
    a2.set_xlabel(r"prime conductor $\ell$")
    a2.set_ylabel("bits")
    a2.set_title("Single-prime vs semiprime type channels")
    a2.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("tower_and_semiprime.png", dpi=150)
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.html:
The Frobenius Clock: how p mod n decides a prime's fate

The units of Z/n sit on a clock. Multiplying by p shuffles them into cycles. The cycle lengths are exactly the degrees of the irreducible factors of the cyclotomic polynomial Φn over Fp.

Frobenius-type distribution (uniform Frobenius)

Full pinning: the type is a function of the residue, so I(residue ; T) = H(T) and H(T | residue) = 0 for every abelian field. What the type forgets is H(residue | T) = log2|G| − H(T). At n = 11 this is exactly 8/5 bits, and H(T) = log25 − 3/5 ≈ 1.72193.

Frobenius classes of p and q are independent and uniform in (Z/ℓ)×. We compute the exact mutual information between the residue of N and the pair of splitting types, compare ordered vs unordered pairs (the "which-factor wall"), and watch finite samples scatter around the exact law.

# Full Pinning at Degree Ten: one remainder, ten symmetries, four fates > **The headline.** For primes $p \neq 11$, the remainder $p \bmod 11$ carries *all* the information about how $p$ splits in the cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$: > $$I(p \bmod 11;\ T) = H(T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35 \approx 1.72193 \text{ bits, exactly.}$$ This page is a guided tour. We begin with a clock, end with semiprimes, and along the way prove why the answer could not have been anything else. --- ## 1. A clock with ten hands The eleventh roots of unity sit on the unit circle. The nontrivial ones are roots of $\Phi_{11}(x) = x^{10} + \cdots + x + 1$, and the symmetries of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ are the maps $\zeta_{11} \mapsto \zeta_{11}^a$ for $a \in (\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$ — a cyclic group of order ten generated by $2$. For a prime $p \ne 11$, the **Frobenius** symmetry is $\zeta_{11} \mapsto \zeta_{11}^p$: it is literally the remainder $p \bmod 11$. Its order $t = \operatorname{ord}_{11}(p)$ — the **Frobenius type** $T(p)$ — decides the prime's fate: $p$ splits into $10/t$ primes of residue degree $t$.
Background: what is a splitting type? In the ring of integers of a number field $K$, a rational prime $p$ factors as a product of prime ideals. If $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois and $p$ unramified, all these ideals have the same residue degree $f$, and there are $[K:\mathbb{Q}]/f$ of them. The residue degree equals the order of the Frobenius element. For cyclotomic fields this is the content of the classical decomposition law; see [cyclotomic fields on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field) and the [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem).
Play with the clock below. Choose a conductor $n$ and a prime $p$. Multiplication by $p$ shuffles the units into cycles — and the cycle lengths are exactly the degrees of the irreducible factors of $\Phi_n$ modulo $p$. {{interactive_demo:0}} Things to try: - At $n = 11$, step through $p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 43$. You will only ever see four patterns: $[1^{10}]$, $[2^5]$, $[5,5]$, $[10]$. - Notice that the bar chart at $n=11$ is always $1, 1, 4, 4$ — Euler's $\varphi(1), \varphi(2), \varphi(5), \varphi(10)$. - Tick *real subfield*: the clock folds in half ($x \sim -x$), the group becomes cyclic of order five, and $H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - 8/5$. --- ## 2. Why the densities are $1, 1, 4, 4$
Theorem (Chebotarev densities of a cyclic field) — click for statement and proof *In a cyclic group of order $n$, exactly $\varphi(d)$ elements have order $d$, for every $d \mid n$. Hence in a cyclic field of degree $n$ the type takes value $d$ with density $\varphi(d)/n$, and* $$H(T) = -\sum_{d \mid n} \frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\log_2 \frac{\varphi(d)}{n}.$$ *Proof.* There is a unique subgroup of order $d$; it is cyclic and its $\varphi(d)$ generators are exactly the elements of order $d$. $\square$
At degree ten: $$H(T) = \tfrac{2}{10}\log_2 10 + \tfrac{8}{10}\log_2\tfrac{10}{4} = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35 \approx 1.72193.$$ The empirical record: on $295{,}946$ unramified primes the observed type frequencies matched $1/10, 1/10, 4/10, 4/10$. The figure below repeats the experiment on all primes below four million, and shows how the $\log_2 10$ bits of the remainder divide into "type bits" and "leftover bits". {{visualization:0}} --- ## 3. Full pinning — and why abelian is the magic word **Abelian full-pinning law.** *For every finite abelian Galois group $A$, every readout $c$ that separates the elements of $A$, and every type readout $T$:* $$I(c;T) = H(T), \qquad H(T \mid c) = 0, \qquad \log_2 |A| - I(c;T) = H(c \mid T).$$
Proof sketch and the non-abelian contrast Because $c$ is injective, $T$ is a function of $c$; so the joint readout $(c, T)$ has the same fibres as $c$, giving $H(c,T) = H(c) = \log_2|A|$, and all three identities follow from $I = H(c) + H(T) - H(c,T)$. The general version holds for any finite group $G$: a residue that reads the coset of the derived subgroup $G'$ sees exactly the image of Frobenius in the abelianization $G/G'$. In a non-abelian group, classes of different orders can share that image, and then $H(T\mid c) > 0$ — pinning fails. In an abelian group $G' = 1$ and nothing is hidden.
At degree ten this gives the three headline constants: $$I(p \bmod 11; T) = \log_2 5 - \tfrac35,\qquad H(T \mid p \bmod 11) = 0, \qquad H(p \bmod 11 \mid T) = \tfrac85.$$ The $8/5$ bits are what the type forgets: it cannot tell $3$ from $4$ from $5$ from $9$. You can recompute these numbers for any conductor with the following routine. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 4. From 400 primes to every prime The experiment verified the factor patterns of $\Phi_{11}$ on 400 primes. (Its first run reported 400/400 *mismatches* — because one side was wrapped in an extra pair of brackets. The patterns themselves were perfect.) The pattern is now a theorem for every conductor: **Factor-pattern theorem.** *For $p \nmid n$ and $t = \operatorname{ord}_n(p)$, $\Phi_n$ factors over $\mathbb{F}_p$ into $\varphi(n)/t$ irreducibles, each of degree $t$. This multiset is the cycle type of $x \mapsto px$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$; in particular $p \equiv q \pmod n$ implies identical patterns.*
Proof sketch A primitive $n$-th root of unity $\eta$ lies in $\mathbb{F}_{p^k}$ iff $n \mid p^k - 1$ iff $t \mid k$, so every root of $\Phi_n$ has degree $t$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$. On the group side, the cycles of $x \mapsto px$ are the cosets of $\langle p \rangle$, all of size $t$. Witnesses at $n=11$: $p=23$ gives $[1^{10}]$, $p=43$ gives $[2^5]$, $p=3$ gives $[5,5]$, $p=2$ gives $[10]$ (so $\Phi_{11}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_2$).
The algorithm below computes the pattern the hard way — by distinct-degree factorization, with no reference to orders — and checks it against the orbit pattern. {{algorithm:1}} --- ## 5. The tower and the extra bit $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})$ contains the real quintic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+ = \mathbb{Q}(2\cos(2\pi/11))$. Its type $T^+$ is $1$ on $\pm 1$ and $5$ elsewhere, so $H(T^+) = \log_2 5 - 8/5$, and the same remainder pins it. Going up the tower adds exactly one bit: $$H(T \mid T^+) = 1 = \log_2 [\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11}) : \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})^+].$$
The CRT explanation $C_{10} \cong C_2 \times C_5$. The order of an element is the product of the orders of its components, the product is injective on $\{1,2\}\times\{1,5\}$, and the components are independent. Entropy is additive over independent readouts, so $$H(T) = H_{C_2} + H_{C_5} = 1 + \left(\log_2 5 - \tfrac85\right).$$
Is the "one extra bit" special to $11$? The left panel below computes the gap $H(T) - H(T^+)$ for many primes and compares it with the *conjectured* law $2^{1 - v_2(\ell - 1)}$ — one bit when $\ell \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, half a bit when $\ell \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, and so on. {{visualization:1}} --- ## 6. Semiprimes: multiplying fates For $N = pq$ with independent uniform Frobenius classes, the remainder $N \bmod 11$ is the *product* of two remainders. The exact channel is $$I\big(N \bmod 11;\ \{T(p),T(q)\}\big) = \log_2 5 + \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 - \tfrac{47}{25} \approx 1.20271.$$
Where the $\log_2 3$ comes from On the 100 equally likely pairs, each square class $N \in \{3,4,5,9\}$ is hit by exactly three ordered pairs of type $(5,5)$ and three of type $(10,10)$; each non-square class $N \in \{2,6,7,8\}$ by six pairs of type $\{5,10\}$. These cells of size $3$ and $6$ are the only source of $\log_2 3$. With $H(N) = \log_2 10$, $H(\text{pair}) = 2\log_2 5 - 93/50$ and $H(N, \text{pair}) = 2\log_2 5 + 51/50 - \frac{12}{25}\log_2 3$, the formula follows.
Three numbers were on the table: a measurement $1.2002$, an enumeration $1.1999$, and an earlier closed-form prediction $1.2027$. The exact law is within $3 \cdot 10^{-5}$ of $1.2027$ and strictly above the other two. In the lab below, draw finite samples and watch plug-in estimates scatter (with a visible bias) around the exact value. Then change the conductor $\ell$. {{interactive_demo:1}} The **attenuation** relative to a single prime is exact: $$H(T) - I_{\text{semi}} = \tfrac{32}{25} - \tfrac{12}{25}\log_2 3 \approx 0.519 \text{ bits.}$$ --- ## 7. The which-factor wall is not there Does knowing *which* factor has which type — the ordered pair — tell you more about $N$? At degree ten: not one bit more. And the reason is structural.
Swap lemma and the wall theorem *Swap lemma.* If an involution $\sigma$ fixes $Y$ and swaps the coordinates of a pair readout $O$, then $H(Y,O) = H(Y, \operatorname{sym}O) + P(O_1 \ne O_2)$: forgetting order costs exactly the off-diagonal probability, one bit per off-diagonal sample. *Wall theorem.* If the residue satisfies $c(gh) = c(hg)$, apply the lemma with $\sigma(g,h) = (h,g)$, once with $Y = c(gh)$ and once with $Y$ constant; the two corrections cancel in the mutual information. This holds in every abelian group, and in every group whose residue is read through the abelianization, since $gh$ and $hg$ differ by the commutator $[g,h]$. It explains the zero walls previously computed for $A_4$ and $D_4$.
The demo checks the theorem on $(\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times$, on $S_3$ and $A_4$ read through their abelianizations — and shows a genuine nonzero wall once the hypotheses are broken. {{demo:1}} --- ## 8. Certified decimals Every decimal on this page is backed by exact integer inequalities such as $2^{23219} < 5^{10000}$ and $3^{100000} < 2^{158497}$, giving $2.3219 < \log_2 5 < 2.32193$ and $1.58496 < \log_2 3 < 1.58497$, hence $1.7219 < H(T) < 1.72193$ and $|I_{\text{semi}} - 1.2027| < 3\cdot 10^{-5}$. {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 9. Everything at once The full numerical companion reproduces every constant of the paper: densities, full pinning, the polynomial check on 400 primes by independent factorization, the tower, the semiprime channel, the certified bounds, and the empirical densities on real primes. {{demo:0}} --- ## Where next? - **Tower-gap law:** is $H(T) - H(T^+) = 2^{1 - v_2(p-1)}$ for every odd prime $p$? - **CRT additivity:** $H_{C_{mn}} = H_{C_m} + H_{C_n}$ for coprime $m, n$. - **Strict attenuation:** is the semiprime channel strictly weaker for every prime conductor $\ell \ge 5$? - **Non-abelian rungs:** how much does an abelian residue miss when the Galois group is not abelian? -- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Cryptography/DegreeTenCyclotomic/Frobenius.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Frobenius factor patterns of cyclotomic polynomials (all conductors)

Built on Mathlib's `Polynomial.natDegree_of_mem_normalizedFactors_cyclotomic`:

* `cyclotomic_factor_degree` — every irreducible factor of `Φₙ` over `𝔽_p` (`p ∤ n`) has
  degree `ord_n(p)`.
* `cyclotomic_factor_pattern` — the factor-degree multiset is `replicate (φ(n)/t) t`.
* `mulLeft_minimalPeriod`, `zpowers_index_mul_orderOf` — the group-side mirror: left
  multiplication by `g` has all cycles of length `ord(g)`, and `|G|/ord(g)` of them.
-/

open Polynomial UniqueFactorizationMonoid

namespace DegreeTen

/-- The Frobenius class of a prime `p ∤ n` in `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/n)ˣ`: the residue `p mod n`. -/
def frobUnit (p n : ℕ) (h : p.Coprime n) : (ZMod n)ˣ := ZMod.unitOfCoprime p h

/-- **Factor-degree law over `𝔽_p`.**  Every irreducible factor of `Φₙ` in `𝔽_p[X]` has degree
equal to the order of the Frobenius class `p mod n`. -/
theorem cyclotomic_factor_degree (p n : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (h : p.Coprime n)
    {P : (ZMod p)[X]} (hP : P ∈ normalizedFactors (cyclotomic n (ZMod p))) :
    P.natDegree = orderOf (frobUnit p n h) := by
  have hK : Fintype.card (ZMod p) = p ^ 1 := by simp [ZMod.card]
  rw [natDegree_of_mem_normalizedFactors_cyclotomic hK h hP]
  congr 1
  ext
  simp [frobUnit]

/-- **The full factor-degree pattern.**  For `p ∤ n`, the multiset of degrees of the monic
irreducible factors of `Φₙ` over `𝔽_p` is `[t, t, …, t]` with `φ(n)/t` entries, where
`t = ord_n(p)`.  (For `n = 11`: `[1¹⁰]`, `[2⁵]`, `[5,5]`, `[10]`.) -/
theorem cyclotomic_factor_pattern (p n : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (h : p.Coprime n) :
    (normalizedFactors (cyclotomic n (ZMod p))).map natDegree =
      Multiset.replicate (n.totient / orderOf (frobUnit p n h)) (orderOf (frobUnit p n h)) := by
  set t := orderOf (frobUnit p n h) with ht
  set F := normalizedFactors (cyclotomic n (ZMod p)) with hF
  have hall : ∀ b ∈ F.map natDegree, b = t := by
    intro b hb
    obtain ⟨P, hP, rfl⟩ := Multiset.mem_map.mp hb
    exact cyclotomic_factor_degree p n h hP
  have hmap : F.map natDegree = Multiset.replicate F.card t := by
    rw [Multiset.eq_replicate]; exact ⟨by simp, hall⟩
  have hdeg : F.card * t = n.totient := by
    have hprod := prod_normalizedFactors (cyclotomic_ne_zero n (ZMod p))
    have H := natDegree_eq_of_degree_eq (degree_eq_degree_of_associated hprod)
    rw [natDegree_cyclotomic, natDegree_multiset_prod _ (zero_notMem_normalizedFactors _)] at H
    rw [← hF, hmap] at H
    simpa [Multiset.sum_replicate] using H
  have htpos : 0 < t := orderOf_pos _
  rw [hmap, ← hdeg, Nat.mul_div_cancel _ htpos]

/-- **Group-side mirror.**  In any finite group, left multiplication by `g` has every point
of exact period `ord(g)`: its cycles all have length `ord(g)`. -/
theorem mulLeft_minimalPeriod {G : Type*} [Group G] (g x : G) :
    Function.minimalPeriod (g * ·) x = orderOf g := by
  rw [orderOf, Function.minimalPeriod_eq_minimalPeriod_iff]
  intro m
  simp only [Function.IsPeriodicPt, Function.IsFixedPt]
  have key : ∀ y : G, (g * ·)^[m] y = g ^ m * y := by
    intro y
    induction m generalizing y with
    | zero => simp
    | succ k ih =>
      rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply', ih, pow_succ', mul_assoc]
  rw [key, key, mul_one]
  constructor
  · intro hx; simpa using hx
  · intro hg; rw [hg, one_mul]

/-- …and there are exactly `|G| / ord(g)` such cycles (cosets of `⟨g⟩`). -/
theorem zpowers_index_mul_orderOf {G : Type*} [Group G] (g : G) :
    (Subgroup.zpowers g).index * orderOf g = Nat.card G := by
  rw [← Nat.card_zpowers, Subgroup.index_mul_card]

end DegreeTen
